Key Factors That Affect Our Results of Operations The following factors have affected, and may continue to affect, our financial condition and results of operations. These factors should be read together with the risk factors and other information included elsewhere in this registration statement. Our ability to secure new project awards We secure projects through customer qualification, tender invitations, technical and commercial submissions, negotiations and formal purchase orders or contract awards. In the three months ended June 30, 2026, we submitted 212 quotations with an aggregate value of $3.9 million and received 61 purchase orders with an aggregate value of $0.8 million, representing conversion rates of approximately 28.8% by number of quotations and 20.0% by aggregate value. During the twelve months ended March 31, 2026, we submitted 705 quotations with an aggregate value of $211.6 million and received 205 purchase orders with an aggregate value of $27.9 million, representing conversion rates of approximately 29.1% by number of quotations and 13.2% by aggregate value. During the twelve months ended March 31, 2025, we submitted 768 quotations with an aggregate value of $261.7 million and received 241 purchase orders with an aggregate value of $56.7 million, representing conversion rates of approximately 31.4% by number of quotations and 21.7% by aggregate value. The period from submission of a quotation to award of a contract has historically been approximately three months, followed by approximately one week from award to project mobilization. Our ability to participate in certain tenders depends on our satisfying applicable customer qualification requirements and maintaining approved-vendor status. Our results of operations in any period may be materially affected by the number and aggregate value of project awards we receive, and historical conversion rates are not necessarily indicative of future awards. 58 Our ability to procure materials and equipment on a timely and cost-effective basis Our project costs and project schedules depend on the availability, delivery lead times and pricing of the specialized construction materials and equipment required for our projects. During the twelve months ended March 31, 2026 and 2025, our procurement activities were primarily affected by the availability and delivery timelines of specialized construction materials and mechanical and electrical equipment required for industrial and cleanroom projects. Our top five suppliers accounted for approximately 20% and 24% of total procurement expenditure in the twelve months ended March 31, 2026 and 2025, respectively. Long-lead items, including uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units, air volume control (AVC) units, vacuum pumps and fire roller shutters, typically required lead times ranging from 14 to 21 weeks. During the periods under review, we experienced extended waiting times for these items, which delayed the progress of certain projects. Our fixed-price contracts generally do not provide for automatic recovery of material price escalation, although we may submit variations and change orders for changes in client requirements or instructions. As of March 31, 2026, we had outstanding purchase commitments of approximately $4.2 million relating to piping and civil and structural works subcontractors. Because our contracts are generally fixed-price, increases in the price of materials or equipment, or delays in their delivery, may increase project costs, delay the timing of revenue recognition and reduce gross margin in the periods affected. Our ability to attract, retain and deploy qualified personnel Our ability to execute projects on schedule depends on our ability to attract, retain and deploy qualified engineering, project management and site personnel. Our average employee workforce increased from approximately 33 employees in the twelve months ended March 31, 2025 to approximately 52 employees in the twelve months ended March 31, 2026, with period-end headcount increasing from 34 to 59 employees, primarily to support the execution of multiple concurrent projects. We strengthened our engineering, project management, site supervision, safety and support functions while increasing our reliance on subcontractors for specialized trades such as civil, mechanical, electrical, HVAC, cleanroom installation and piping works in order to meet project schedules. Project activity during the twelve months ended March 31, 2026 required significant overtime, particularly for engineering, site supervision, safety, quality assurance and quality control and commercial personnel supporting fast-track projects, which increased our staffing costs for the period. As resources were prioritized for project execution, most technical and professional training programs were deferred to the twelve months ending March 31, 2027. We expect to resume regular training as project workloads normalize. Our ability to strengthen our competitive advantages Our operating results depend in part on our ability to maintain and strengthen competitive advantages in providing construction and maintenance services for high-tech production facilities. Customers rely on us to support the construction and maintenance of production facilities that may require specialized project execution, technical coordination, quality control and compliance with customer specifications. Our ability to apply technical know-how, execute projects on schedule, meet customer performance requirements and maintain our reputation with customers directly affects our profitability and our ability to secure additional projects. Our ability to control costs and improve operating efficiency Our profitability depends substantially on our ability to control project costs, staffing costs and administrative expenses while maintaining customer service quality and project execution standards. Construction costs, including purchased construction, subcontractor expenses, materials, salaries and welfare, and outsourcing expenses, have a direct impact on profitability. In addition, staffing costs and administrative expenses affect profitability and operating leverage. Our ability to attract and retain qualified employees, identify business opportunities, secure new customer contracts, control procurement costs, manage subcontractors and improve employee productivity affects our margins and operating results. Project timing, percentage-of-completion revenue recognition and working capital Our results may vary significantly from period to period because revenue recognition, gross profit, contract assets, deferred revenue, retention receivables and operating cash flows depend on project commencement, progress toward completion, customer approvals, billing milestones, collection timing, procurement timing and subcontractor payment terms. Critical Accounting Policies, Judgments and Estimates Our consolidated financial statements are prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP. The preparation of these financial statements requires management to make estimates and judgments that affect the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses. Actual results may differ from these estimates. We periodically review our estimates and assumptions based on available information. The accounting policies that involve the most significant judgments and estimates, and that may materially affect our financial condition and results of operations, primarily relate to revenue recognition and project estimates, accounts receivable and other asset recoverability, long-lived assets, and contingent liabilities. 71 Revenue Recognition and Project Estimates We derive substantially all of our revenue from construction contracts. Revenue is generally recognized over time as we satisfy our performance obligations, with progress measured primarily using the cost-to-cost method. This method requires management to estimate total contract revenue and costs, including the effect of change orders, claims, incentives, penalties and other variable consideration. Because these estimates may change as projects progress, revisions to estimated contract revenue or costs may result in cumulative catch-up adjustments to revenue and profit in the period of change. If estimated total contract costs exceed the transaction price, the expected loss is recognized immediately. Accordingly, the accuracy of our revenue and profit recognition depends significantly on the accuracy of our project estimates. Accounts Receivable and Other Asset Recoverability We assess the collectability of accounts receivable and other assets based on factors such as customers’ financial condition, historical collection experience, aging of balances and other relevant information. We record allowances when amounts are not expected to be fully recoverable. Long-Lived Assets and Contingent Liabilities We evaluate long-lived assets for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate that their carrying amounts may not be recoverable. We also assess potential contingent liabilities based on the facts and circumstances available at the reporting date and recognize provisions when required under applicable U.S. GAAP. Foreign Currency Translation Our reporting currency is the U.S. dollar, while our functional currency is the Malaysian Ringgit. Financial statement balances and transactions denominated in currencies other than the functional currency are translated in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Foreign currency movements may therefore affect reported results and shareholders’ equity. Duties of Directors Under Cayman Islands law, all of Holdco’s directors owe three types of duties to Holdco: (i) statutory duties, (ii) fiduciary duties, and (iii) common law duties. The Cayman Companies Act imposes a number of statutory duties on a director. A Cayman Islands director’s fiduciary duties are not codified, however, the courts of the Cayman Islands have held that a director owes the following fiduciary duties: (a) a duty to act in what the director bona fide considers to be in the best interests of the company, (b) a duty to exercise their powers for the purposes they were conferred, (c) a duty to avoid fettering his or her discretion in the future and (d) a duty to avoid conflicts of interest and of duty. The common law duties owed by a director are those to act with skill, care and diligence that may reasonably be expected of a person carrying out the same functions as are carried out by that director in relation to the company and, also, to act with the skill, care and diligence in keeping with a standard of care commensurate with any particular skill they have which enables them to meet a higher standard than a director without those skills. In fulfilling their duty of care to Holdco, Holdco’s directors must ensure compliance with Holdco’s Amended and Restated Memorandum and Articles of Association. Holdco has the right to seek damages if a duty owed by any of its directors is breached. Section 145 of the Delaware General Corporation Law provides that a corporation may indemnify directors and officers as well as other employees and individuals against expenses including attorneys’ fees, judgments, fines and amounts paid in settlement in connection with various actions, suits or proceedings, whether civil, criminal, administrative or investigative other than an action by or in the right of the corporation, a derivative action, if they acted in good faith and in a manner they reasonably believed to be in or not opposed to the best interests of the corporation, and, with respect to any criminal action or proceeding, if they had no reasonable cause to believe their conduct was unlawful. A similar standard is applicable in the case of derivative actions, except that indemnification only extends to expenses including attorneys’ fees incurred in connection with the defense or settlement of such actions, and the statute requires court approval before there can be any indemnification where the person seeking indemnification has been found liable to the corporation. The statute provides that it is not exclusive of other indemnification that may be granted by a corporation’s certificate of incorporation, bylaws, agreement, a vote of stockholders or disinterested directors or otherwise. The Company’s Certificate of Incorporation provides that it will indemnify and hold harmless, to the fullest extent permitted by Section 145 of the Delaware General Corporation Law, as amended from time to time, each person that such section grants us the power to indemnify. The Delaware General Corporation Law permits a corporation to provide in its certificate of incorporation that a director of the corporation shall not be personally liable to the corporation or its stockholders for monetary damages for breach of fiduciary duty as a director, except for liability for: ● any breach of the director’s duty of loyalty to the corporation or its stockholders; ● acts or omissions not in good faith or which involve intentional misconduct or a knowing violation of law; ● payments of unlawful dividends or unlawful stock repurchases or redemptions; or ● any transaction from which the director derived an improper personal benefit. The Company’s Certificate of Incorporation provides that, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, none of our directors will be personally liable to us or our stockholders for monetary damages for breach of fiduciary duty as a director. (the “Company”) is a blank check company incorporated in the State of Delaware on April 16, 2021. The Company was formed for the purpose of acquiring, engaging in a share exchange, share reconstruction and amalgamation with, purchasing all or substantially all of the assets of, entering into contractual arrangements with, or engaging in any other similar business combination with one or more businesses or entities (a “Business Combination”). All activity from April 16, 2021 (inception) through December 31, 2025, relates to the Company’s formation, the Initial Public Offering (as defined below), and its pursuit of an initial Business Combination. The Company will not generate any operating revenues until after the completion of its initial Business Combination, at the earliest. The Company will generate non-operating income in the form of interest income on cash and cash equivalents from the proceeds derived from the Initial Public Offering. The Company has selected December 31 as its fiscal year end. The Company is an early stage and emerging growth company and, as such, the Company is subject to all of the risks associated with early stage and emerging growth companies. The Company’s sponsor is Broad Capital LLC, a Delaware limited liability company (the “Sponsor”). The registration statement for the Company’s Initial Public Offering was declared effective on January 10, 2022. On January 13, 2022, the Company closed its Initial Public Offering of 10,000,000 units (the “Units” and, with respect to the shares of common stock included in the Units being offered, the “Public Shares”), at $10.00 per Unit, generating gross proceeds of $100,000,000 (the “Initial Public Offering”), and incurring transaction costs of $6,917,226, of which $3,500,000 was for deferred underwriting commissions (see Note 7). The Company granted the underwriter a 45-day option to purchase up to 1,500,000 Units at the Initial Public Offering price to cover over-allotments, if any. On February 9, 2022, the Underwriters partially exercised the over-allotment option and on February 10, 2022, purchased an additional 159,069 Units from the Company (the “Over-Allotment Units”), generating gross proceeds of $1,590,690, and forfeited the remainder of the option. Simultaneously with the consummation of the closing of the Initial Public Offering, the Company consummated the private placement of an aggregate of 446,358 units (the “Placement Units”) to the Sponsor at a price of $10.00 per Placement Unit, generating total gross proceeds of $4,463,580 (the “Private Placement”) (see Note 4). With the exercise of the Over-Allotment Units, the Company consummated the Private Placement of 4,772 Placement Units to the Sponsor generating gross proceeds of $47,720. On February 9, 2022, the underwriters partially exercised the over-allotment option and purchased an additional 159,069 Units, generating gross proceeds of $1,590,690 and forfeited the remainder of the option, which is 335,233 shares of common stock. In connection with the closing and sale of the Over-Allotment Units and the additional Placement Units (together, the “Over-Allotment Closing”), a total of $1,606,597 in proceeds from the Over-Allotment Closing (which amount includes $31,814 of the Underwriters’ deferred discount) was placed in a U.S.-based trust account established for the benefit of the Company’s public stockholders, maintained by Continental Stock Transfer & Trust Company, acting as trustee. Following the closing of the Initial Public Offering on January 13, 2022, an amount of $101,000,000 ($10.10 per Unit) from the net proceeds of the sale of the Units in the Initial Public Offering and a portion of the proceeds from the sale of the Placement Units was placed in a trust account (the “Trust Account”), located in the United States and held as cash items or may be invested in U.S. government securities, within the meaning set forth in Section 2(a)(16) of the Investment Company Act, with a maturity of 185 days or less, or in any open-ended investment company that holds itself out as a money market fund meeting the conditions of Rule 2a-7 of the Investment Company Act, as determined by the Company, until the earlier of: (i) the consummation of a Business Combination or (ii) the distribution of the funds in the Trust Account to the Company’s stockholders, as described below. Redemption Option The Company will provide the holders of the outstanding Public Shares (the “Public Stockholders”) with the opportunity to redeem all or a portion of their Public Shares either (i) in connection with a stockholders meeting called to approve the Business Combination or (ii) by means of a tender offer in connection with the Business Combination. The decision as to whether the Company will seek stockholder approval of a Business Combination or conduct a tender offer, will be made by the Company. The Public Stockholders will be entitled to redeem their Public Shares for a pro rata portion of the amount then in the Trust Account (initially anticipated to be $10.10 per Public Share, plus any pro rata interest then in the Trust Account, net of taxes payable). The Public Shares subject to redemption will be recorded at a redemption value and classified as temporary equity upon the completion of the Initial Public Offering in accordance with the Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) Topic 480 “ Distinguishing Liabilities from Equity ”. The Company will not redeem Public Shares in an amount that would cause its net tangible assets to be less than $5,000,001 (so that it does not then become subject to the SEC’s “penny stock” rules) or any greater net tangible asset or cash requirement which may be contained in the agreement relating to the Business Combination. If the Company seeks stockholder approval of the Business Combination, the Company will proceed with a Business Combination if a majority of the outstanding shares voted are voted in favor of the Business Combination, or such other vote as required by law or stock exchange rule. If a stockholder vote is not required by applicable law or stock exchange listing requirements and the Company does not decide to hold a stockholder vote for business or other reasons, the Company will, pursuant to its second amended and restated certificate of incorporation (the “Certificate of Incorporation”), conduct the redemptions pursuant to the tender offer rules of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) and file tender offer documents with the SEC prior to completing a Business Combination. Emerging Growth Company The Company is an “emerging growth company,” as defined in Section 2(a) of the Securities Act, as modified by the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act of 2012 (the “JOBS Act”), and it may take advantage of certain exemptions from various reporting requirements that are applicable to other public companies that are not emerging growth companies including, but not limited to, not being required to comply with the auditor attestation requirements of Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, reduced disclosure obligations regarding executive compensation in its periodic reports and proxy statements, and exemptions from the requirements of holding a nonbinding advisory vote on executive compensation and stockholder approval of any golden parachute payments not previously approved. Further, Section 102(b)(1) of the JOBS Act exempts emerging growth companies from being required to comply with new or revised financial accounting standards until private companies (that is, those that have not had a Securities Act registration statement declared effective or do not have a class of securities registered under the Exchange Act) are required to comply with the new or revised financial accounting standards. The JOBS Act provides that a company can elect to opt out of the extended transition period and comply with the requirements that apply to non-emerging growth companies but any such election to opt out is irrevocable. The Company has elected not to opt out of such extended transition period which means that when a standard is issued or revised and it has different application dates for public or private companies, the Company, as an emerging growth company, can adopt the new or revised standard at the time private companies adopt the new or revised standard. This may make comparison of the Company’s financial statements with another public company which is neither an emerging growth company nor an emerging growth company which has opted out of using the extended transition period difficult or impossible because of the potential differences in accounting standards used. F- 14 Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 On August 16, 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (the “IR Act”) was signed into federal law. The IR Act provides for, among other things, a new U.S. federal 1% excise tax on certain repurchases (including redemptions) of stock by publicly traded domestic (i.e., U.S.) corporations and certain domestic subsidiaries of publicly traded foreign corporations. The excise tax is imposed on the repurchasing corporation itself, not its stockholders from which shares are repurchased. The amount of the excise tax is generally 1% of the fair market value of the shares repurchased at the time of the repurchase. However, for purposes of calculating the excise tax, repurchasing corporations are permitted to net the fair market value of certain new stock issuances against the fair market value of stock repurchases during the same taxable year. In addition, certain exceptions apply to the excise tax. The U.S. Department of the Treasury (the “Treasury”) has been given authority to provide regulations and other guidance to carry out and prevent the abuse or avoidance of the excise tax. The IR Act applies only to repurchases that occur after December 31, 2022. Any redemption or other repurchase that occurs after December 31, 2022, in connection with a Business Combination, extension vote or otherwise, may be subject to the excise tax. Whether and to what extent the Company would be subject to the excise tax in connection with a Business Combination, extension vote or otherwise would depend on a number of factors, including (i) the fair market value of the redemptions and repurchases in connection with the Business Combination, extension or otherwise, (ii) the structure of a Business Combination, (iii) the nature and amount of any “PIPE” or other equity issuances in connection with a Business Combination (or otherwise issued not in connection with a Business Combination but issued within the same taxable year of a Business Combination) and (iv) the content of regulations and other guidance from the Treasury. In addition, because the excise tax would be payable by the Company and not by the redeeming holders, the mechanics of any required payment of the excise tax have not been determined. The foregoing could cause a reduction in the cash available on hand to complete a Business Combination and in the Company’s ability to complete a Business Combination. On November 24, 2025, the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (“IRS”) issued final regulations under Internal Revenue Code (“IRC”) Section 4501 (Treasury Decision 10037). Under these final regulations, transition relief from the Excise Tax under Section 4501 is appropriate for certain types of stock issued prior to the date of enactment of the IRA if the covered corporation no longer has discretion as to whether to repurchase such stock after that date. These final regulations specifically incorporate transition relief for mandatorily redeemable stock and for stock subject by its terms to a unilateral put option of the holder, if such stock was outstanding prior to August 16, 2022. While we previously believed that the Excise Tax may have applied to redemptions of our common stock in connection, based on the November 24, 2025, final regulations described above, we no longer believe the Excise Tax applies to the Company’s prior common stock redemptions, since those redemptions occurred solely with respect to redeemable stock issued by the Company in its original IPO in January 2022, such that those redemptions are not treated as stock repurchases for purposes of IRC Section 4501 because that stock was outstanding prior to August 16, 2022. Fair value is defined as the price that would be received for sale of an asset or paid for transfer of a liability, in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. GAAP establishes a three-tier fair value hierarchy, which prioritizes the inputs used in measuring fair value. The hierarchy gives the highest priority to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities (Level 1 measurements) and the lowest priority to unobservable inputs (Level 3 measurements). These tiers include: ● Level 1, defined as observable inputs such as quoted prices (unadjusted) for identical instruments in active markets; ● Level 2, defined as inputs other than quoted prices in active markets that are either directly or indirectly observable such as quoted prices for similar instruments in active markets or quoted prices for identical or similar instruments in markets that are not active; and ● Level 3, defined as unobservable inputs in which little or no market data exists, therefore requiring an entity to develop its own assumptions, such as valuations derived from valuation techniques in which one or more significant inputs or significant value drivers are unobservable. SEGMENT INFORMATION ASC Topic 280, “Segment Reporting,” establishes standards for companies to report in their financial statement information about operating segments, products, services, geographic areas, and major customers. Operating segments are defined as components of an enterprise for which separate financial information is available that is regularly evaluated by the Company’s chief operating decision maker, or group, in deciding how to allocate resources and assess performance. The Company’s chief operating decision maker has been identified as the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Finance Officer (“CODM”), who reviews the operating results for the Company as a whole to make decisions about allocating resources and assessing financial performance. Accordingly, management has determined that the Company only has one operating segment. When evaluating the Company’s performance and making key decisions regarding resource allocation, the CODM reviews key metrics, general, administrative and operational costs and interest income earned on investment held in Trust Account which include the accompanying statement of operations. The CODM reviews interest earned on investment held in Trust Account to measure and monitor shareholder value and determine the most effective strategy of investment with the Trust Account funds while maintaining compliance with the trust agreement. General, administrative and operational costs are reviewed and monitored by the CODM to manage and forecast cash to ensure enough capital is available to complete a business combination within the business combination period. The CODM also reviews general, administrative and operational costs to manage, maintain and enforce all contractual agreements to ensure costs are aligned with all agreements and budget. The CODM also specifically reviews professional service fees in connection with the business combination, which are a significant segment expense as these represent significant costs affecting the Company’s consummation of the business combination. Emerging Growth Company The Company is an “emerging growth company,” as defined in Section 2(a) of the Securities Act, as modified by the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act of 2012 (the “JOBS Act”), and it may take advantage of certain exemptions from various reporting requirements that are applicable to other public companies that are not emerging growth companies including, but not limited to, not being required to comply with the auditor attestation requirements of Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, reduced disclosure obligations regarding executive compensation in its periodic reports and proxy statements, and exemptions from the requirements of holding a nonbinding advisory vote on executive compensation and stockholder approval of any golden parachute payments not previously approved. Further, Section 102(b)(1) of the JOBS Act exempts emerging growth companies from being required to comply with new or revised financial accounting standards until private companies (that is, those that have not had a Securities Act registration statement declared effective or do not have a class of securities registered under the Exchange Act) are required to comply with the new or revised financial accounting standards. The JOBS Act provides that a company can elect to opt out of the extended transition period and comply with the requirements that apply to non-emerging growth companies but any such election to opt out is irrevocable. The Company has elected not to opt out of such extended transition period which means that when a standard is issued or revised and it has different application dates for public or private companies, the Company, as an emerging growth company, can adopt the new or revised standard at the time private companies adopt the new or revised standard. This may make comparison of the Company’s financial statements with another public company which is neither an emerging growth company nor an emerging growth company which has opted out of using the extended transition period difficult or impossible because of the potential differences in accounting standards used. Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 On August 16, 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (the “IR Act”) was signed into federal law. The IR Act provides for, among other things, a new U.S. federal 1 % excise tax on certain repurchases (including redemptions) of stock by publicly traded domestic (i.e., U.S.) corporations and certain domestic subsidiaries of publicly traded foreign corporations. The excise tax is imposed on the repurchasing corporation itself, not its stockholders from which shares are repurchased. The amount of the excise tax is generally 1 % of the fair market value of the shares repurchased at the time of the repurchase. However, for purposes of calculating the excise tax, repurchasing corporations are permitted to net the fair market value of certain new stock issuances against the fair market value of stock repurchases during the same taxable year. In addition, certain exceptions apply to the excise tax. The U.S. Department of the Treasury (the “Treasury”) has been given authority to provide regulations and other guidance to carry out and prevent the abuse or avoidance of the excise tax. The IR Act applies only to repurchases that occur after December 31, 2022. Any redemption or other repurchase that occurs after December 31, 2022, in connection with a Business Combination, extension vote or otherwise, may be subject to the excise tax. Whether and to what extent the Company would be subject to the excise tax in connection with a Business Combination, extension vote or otherwise would depend on a number of factors, including (i) the fair market value of the redemptions and repurchases in connection with the Business Combination, extension or otherwise, (ii) the structure of a Business Combination, (iii) the nature and amount of any “PIPE” or other equity issuances in connection with a Business Combination (or otherwise issued not in connection with a Business Combination but issued within the same taxable year of a Business Combination) and (iv) the content of regulations and other guidance from the Treasury. In addition, because the excise tax would be payable by the Company and not by the redeeming holders, the mechanics of any required payment of the excise tax have not been determined. The foregoing could cause a reduction in the cash available on hand to complete a Business Combination and in the Company’s ability to complete a Business Combination. Fair value is defined as the price that would be received for sale of an asset or paid for transfer of a liability, in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. GAAP establishes a three-tier fair value hierarchy, which prioritizes the inputs used in measuring fair value. The hierarchy gives the highest priority to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities (Level 1 measurements) and the lowest priority to unobservable inputs (Level 3 measurements). These tiers include: ● Level 1, defined as observable inputs such as quoted prices (unadjusted) for identical instruments in active markets; ● Level 2, defined as inputs other than quoted prices in active markets that are either directly or indirectly observable such as quoted prices for similar instruments in active markets or quoted prices for identical or similar instruments in markets that are not active; and ● Level 3, defined as unobservable inputs in which little or no market data exists, therefore requiring an entity to develop its own assumptions, such as valuations derived from valuation techniques in which one or more significant inputs or significant value drivers are unobservable. The Company, through its wholly owned subsidiary, Conwall Malaysia, is engaged in the business of providing construction and maintenance services. The Company and its subsidiary are collectively referred to as the “Group” or the “Company”. Where appropriate, the terms “we,” “our,” and “us” refer collectively to Conwall and its subsidiary. The Company evaluates the collectability of its accounts receivable on a recurring basis and maintains adequate allowance for expected credit losses based on management’s estimate of lifetime expected credit losses. In estimating the allowance, the Company considers historical collection experience, the aging of receivable balances, customers’ financial condition and creditworthiness, current economic conditions, reasonable and supportable forecasts, and other relevant factors that may affect customers’ ability to pay. Accounts receivable are written off against the allowance when management determines that collection is not probable. Subsequent recoveries of amounts previously written off are recorded by reversing the allowance and reducing bad debt expense in the period received. Advance Payments Advance payments represent amounts paid to material suppliers and subcontractors in accordance with the terms of purchase contracts and subcontract agreements. These payments are applied against future billings from the respective suppliers and subcontractors as materials are delivered or services are performed. Advance payments are classified as current or non-current assets based on the Company’s expectation of when the related goods or services will be received and the advances will be applied. Amounts expected to be applied within one year after the balance sheet date are classified as current assets, while amounts expected to be applied after one year are classified as non-current assets. Project Retention Project retention represents the portion of the contract price withheld by customers from progress payments on completed construction projects. These retentions serve as security for the satisfactory performance of the Company’s contractual obligations, including any defects or warranty claims. Retained amounts are generally released to the Company in accordance with the terms of the respective contracts, typically within one to two years after project completion upon the expiry of the warranty or defect liability period. Project retentions are classified as current or non-current, depending on the expected release date, and are stated at their original amount less any allowance for doubtful accounts, if required. The Company periodically reviews the collectability of project retentions and recognizes an allowance when there is objective evidence that the amounts may not be fully recoverable. Write-offs and recoveries are accounted for in the same manner as accounts receivable. F- 53 CONWALL CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRIES LIMITED AND SUBSIDIARY NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS Note 2- SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (continued) Revenue Recognition The Company adopted ASC 606 upon inception. Under ASC 606, revenue is recognized when a customer obtains control of promised goods or services, in an amount that reflects the consideration which the entity expects to receive in exchange for those goods or services. To determine revenue recognition for arrangements that an entity determines are within the scope of ASC 606, the Company performs the following five steps: (i) identify the contract(s) with a customer; (ii) identify the performance obligations in the contract; (iii) determine the transaction price; (iv) allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations in the contract; and (v) recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation. The Company derives its revenue primarily from construction contracts with customers. Revenue is recognized in accordance with ASC 606 when control of the promised goods or services is transferred to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration the Company expects to receive in exchange for those goods or services. Construction contracts generally contain a single performance obligation because the individual services provided under the contract are not separately identifiable and are integrated into a single combined output, which is the completed construction project. Revenue from construction contracts is recognized over time, as the Company’s performance creates or enhances an asset that the customer controls as the asset is constructed. Progress toward completion is measured using the cost-to-cost input method, under which the percentage of completion is determined by comparing costs incurred to date with total estimated contract costs. Revenue recognized to date is calculated by applying the percentage of completion to the total transaction price of the contract. Revenue recognized in the current period represents the cumulative revenue recognized to date less amounts recognized in prior periods. Costs incurred include direct materials, direct labor, subcontractor costs, and other costs directly attributable to the contract. Management periodically reviews and updates estimates of total contract costs. Changes in estimated costs or contract value are recognized as cumulative catch-up adjustments to revenue in the period the estimates change. Timing differences between revenue recognized and amounts billed to customers result in contract assets or contract liabilities. A contract asset is recorded when revenue recognized exceeds billings to the customer, while a contract liability is recorded when billings exceed revenue recognized. The Company expects substantially all contract assets outstanding as of March 31, 2026 to be billed and collected within one year. The Company also expects substantially all contract liabilities outstanding as of March 31, 2026 to be recognized as revenue within one year. If at any time the estimated total costs of a contract exceed the transaction price, the Company recognizes the entire estimated loss immediately in the period in which the loss becomes probable. F- 54 CONWALL CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRIES LIMITED AND SUBSIDIARY NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS Note 2- SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (continued) Revenue Recognition (continued) For certain sundry construction projects with a total contract price of less than $ 24,020 (RM 100,000 ) or an expected duration of less than three months , the Company does not apply the cost-to-cost input method to measure progress toward completion. Due to the short-term nature and immaterial size of these contracts, revenue is recognized by matching revenue with the related costs incurred within the same reporting period. Management has concluded that this approach does not result in a material difference from the revenue that would have been recognized using the cost-to-cost input method. The Company generally provides limited warranties for work performed under its contracts. These warranties are assurance-type warranties that provide customers with assurance that the completed work complies with agreed-upon specifications and do not represent separate performance obligations. Historically, warranty claims have not resulted in material costs incurred. Any estimated warranty costs are included in the individual project cost estimates used in accounting for long-term contracts. Project Estimates Due to the nature of our industry, there is significant complexity in our estimation of total expected revenue and cost, for which we must make significant judgments. Our contracts with our customers may contain several types of variable consideration, including claims, unpriced change orders, award and incentive fees, liquidated damages and penalties or other provisions that can either increase or decrease the contract price to arrive at estimated revenue. Certain variable consideration, such as award and incentive fees, generally are earned upon achievement of certain performance metrics, program milestones or cost targets and can be based upon customer discretion. We estimate variable consideration at the most likely amount to which we expect to be entitled upon completion of a project. We include estimated amounts in the transaction price to the extent it is probable we will realize that amount. Our estimates of variable consideration and our determination of its inclusion in project revenue are based on an assessment of our anticipated performance and other information that may be available to us. At a project level, we have specific practices and procedures to review our estimate of total revenue and cost. Each project team reviews the progress and execution of our performance obligations, which impact the project’s accounting outcome. As part of this process, the project team reviews information such as any outstanding key contract matters, progress towards completion and the related program schedule and identified risks and opportunities. The accuracy of our revenue and profit recognition in a given period depends on the accuracy of our project estimates, which can change from period to period due to a variety of factors including: ● Complexity in original design; ● Extent of changes from original design; ● Different site conditions than assumed in our bid; ● Length of time to complete the project; ● Availability and cost of equipment and materials; ● Subcontractor performance; ● Our ability to recover for additional contract costs. We recognize changes in contract estimates on a cumulative catch-up basis in the period in which the changes are identified. Such changes in contract estimates can result in the recognition of revenue in a current period for performance obligations which were satisfied or partially satisfied in prior periods. Changes in contract estimates may also result in the reversal of previously recognized revenue if the current estimate adversely differs from the previous estimate. F- 56 CONWALL CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRIES LIMITED AND SUBSIDIARY NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS Note 2- SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (continued) Income Taxes The Company accounts for current income taxes in accordance with the laws of the relevant tax authorities. Deferred income taxes are recognized when temporary differences exist between the tax bases of assets and liabilities and their reported amounts in the consolidated financial statements. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates expected to apply to taxable income in the years in which those temporary differences are expected to be recovered or settled. The effect on deferred tax assets and liabilities of a change in tax rates is recognized in income in the period including the enactment date. Valuation allowances are established, when necessary, to reduce deferred tax assets to the amount expected to be realized. An uncertain tax position is recognized only if it is “more likely than not” that the tax position would be sustained in a tax examination. The amount recognized is the largest amount of tax benefit that is greater than 50% likely of being realized on examination. For tax positions not meeting the “more likely than not” test, no tax benefit is recorded. Penalties and interest incurred related to underpayment of income tax are classified as income tax expense in the period incurred. (1) Income tax of Cayman Islands Conwall was incorporated in the Cayman Islands as an exempted company and is governed by the tax laws of the Cayman Islands. Under the current laws of the Cayman Islands, Conwall is not subject to income taxes or capital gains taxes. In addition, upon payment of dividends by Conwall to its shareholders, no Cayman Islands withholding tax will be imposed. (2) Income tax of Malaysia Conwall Malaysia was incorporated in Malaysia, and accordingly are governed by the income tax laws of Malaysia. The income tax provision in respect of operations in Malaysia is calculated at the applicable tax rates on the taxable income for the periods based on existing legislation, interpretations, and practices. Under the Income Tax Act of Malaysia, enterprises incorporated in Malaysia are usually subject to a unified 24 % enterprise income tax rate while prefer, tax holidays, and tax exemptions may be granted on a case-by-case basis. The tax rate for small and medium sized companies (generally companies incorporated in Malaysia with paid-in capital of $617,711 (RM2,500,000) or less, and gross income of not more than $12,010,280 (RM50,000,000) is 15% on the first $36,030 (RM150,000) of taxable income and 17% on taxable income from $36,031 (RM150,001) to $144,123 (RM600,000), with any remaining taxable income taxed at the standard rate of 24% . The local tax authority conducts periodic and ad hoc tax filing reviews on business enterprises after those enterprises complete their relevant tax filings. Therefore, the Company’s tax filings are subject to examination. It is therefore uncertain as to whether the local tax authority may take different views about the Company’s tax filings, which may lead to additional tax liabilities. As of March 31, 2026 and 2025, all of the Company’s tax returns remain open for statutory examination by relevant tax authorities. Conwall Malaysia evaluates its uncertain tax positions in accordance with applicable accounting guidance. The Company recognizes interest and penalties related to uncertain tax positions, if any, as a component of income tax expense. As of March 31, 2026, the Company did not have any significant uncertain tax positions requiring recognition or disclosure in the accompanying consolidated financial statements. Conwall Malaysia is engaged in the business of construction services, which became subject to certain construction-related service tax on July 1, 2025. Conwall registered with the local tax authorities in August 2025 and commenced filing service tax returns and remitting service tax beginning in September 2025. For construction-related services, the applicable service tax rates are 6 % ad valorem for construction work and 8 % ad valorem for maintenance or repair work. A company is required to register for service tax purposes if the total value of its taxable services over a rolling 12-month period exceeds, or is expected to exceed, the prescribed registration threshold of $ 370,627 (RM 1,500,000 ) for construction service providers. Service tax collected is not an expense of the Company and is recorded as a liability until remitted to the Malaysian tax authorities. The Company presents revenue net of service tax collected. Payroll Taxes and Statutory Contributions Under Malaysian income tax regulations, employers are required to withhold employee income taxes under the Monthly Tax Deduction (“MTD”), also known as Potongan Cukai Bulanan (“PCB”), system administered by the Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia. The Company withholds the required amounts from employees’ salaries and remits them to the Malaysian tax authorities on a monthly basis. As the Company acts solely as a withholding agent, amounts withheld from employees’ compensation are not recognized as an expense of the Company and are recorded as payroll tax payable until remitted. In addition to employee income tax withholdings, the Company is required to make statutory employer contributions to employee benefit programs, including the Employees Provident Fund (“EPF”), the Social Security Organization (“SOCSO”), the Employment Insurance System (“EIS”), and, where applicable, the Human Resource Development Corporation (“HRD Corp”). Employer contributions are recognized as employee benefit expense in the period in which the related services are rendered. Amounts due but not yet remitted are included in accrued payroll-related liabilities. HRD Corp administers Malaysia’s Human Resources Development Fund, which is financed through a statutory levy paid by eligible employers. Employers subject to the levy may apply for grants or reimbursements for qualifying employee training and workforce development programs. Levies paid to HRD Corp are recognized as employee benefit expense, while reimbursements received for approved training programs are recognized as a reduction of the related training expense or as other operating income, as appropriate, when realization is probable. Project Retention Project retention represents the portion of the contract price withheld by customers from progress payments on completed construction projects. Project retentions are classified as current or non-current, depending on the expected release date, and are stated at their original amount less any allowance for doubtful accounts, if required. F- 80 CONWALL CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRIES LIMITED AND SUBSIDIARY NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (Unaudited) Note 2- SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (continued) Revenue Recognition The Company adopted ASC 606 upon inception. Under ASC 606, revenue is recognized when a customer obtains control of promised goods or services, in an amount that reflects the consideration which the entity expects to receive in exchange for those goods or services. To determine revenue recognition for arrangements that an entity determines are within the scope of ASC 606, the Company performs the following five steps: (i) identify the contract(s) with a customer; (ii) identify the performance obligations in the contract; (iii) determine the transaction price; (iv) allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations in the contract; and (v) recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation. The Company derives its revenue primarily from construction contracts with customers. Revenue is recognized in accordance with ASC 606 when control of the promised goods or services is transferred to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration the Company expects to receive in exchange for those goods or services. Construction contracts generally contain a single performance obligation because the individual services provided under the contract are not separately identifiable and are integrated into a single combined output, which is the completed construction project. Revenue from construction contracts is recognized over time, as the Company’s performance creates or enhances an asset that the customer controls as the asset is constructed. Progress toward completion is measured using the cost-to-cost input method, under which the percentage of completion is determined by comparing costs incurred to date with total estimated contract costs. Revenue recognized to date is calculated by applying the percentage of completion to the total transaction price of the contract. Revenue recognized in the current period represents the cumulative revenue recognized to date less amounts recognized in prior periods. Costs incurred include direct materials, direct labor, subcontractor costs, and other costs directly attributable to the contract. Management periodically reviews and updates estimates of total contract costs. Changes in estimated costs or contract value are recognized as cumulative catch-up adjustments to revenue in the period the estimates change. Timing differences between revenue recognized and amounts billed to customers result in contract assets or contract liabilities. A contract asset is recorded when revenue recognized exceeds billings to the customer, while a contract liability is recorded when billings exceed revenue recognized. The Company expects substantially all contract assets outstanding as of June 30, 2026 to be billed and collected within one year. The Company also expects substantially all contract liabilities outstanding as of June 30, 2026 to be recognized as revenue within one year. If at any time the estimated total costs of a contract exceed the transaction price, the Company recognizes the entire estimated loss immediately in the period in which the loss becomes probable. Due to the short-term nature and immaterial size of these contracts, revenue is recognized by matching revenue with the related costs incurred within the same reporting period. Management has concluded that this approach does not result in a material difference from the revenue that would have been recognized using the cost-to-cost input method. The Company generally provides limited warranties for work performed under its contracts. These warranties are assurance-type warranties that provide customers with assurance that the completed work complies with agreed-upon specifications and do not represent separate performance obligations. Historically, warranty claims have not resulted in material costs incurred. Any estimated warranty costs are included in the individual project cost estimates used in accounting for long-term contracts. Project Estimates Due to the nature of our industry, there is significant complexity in our estimation of total expected revenue and cost, for which we must make significant judgments. Our contracts with our customers may contain several types of variable consideration, including claims, unpriced change orders, award and incentive fees, liquidated damages and penalties or other provisions that can either increase or decrease the contract price to arrive at estimated revenue. Certain variable consideration, such as award and incentive fees, generally are earned upon achievement of certain performance metrics, program milestones or cost targets and can be based upon customer discretion. We estimate variable consideration at the most likely amount to which we expect to be entitled upon completion of a project. We include estimated amounts in the transaction price to the extent it is probable we will realize that amount. Our estimates of variable consideration and our determination of its inclusion in project revenue are based on an assessment of our anticipated performance and other information that may be available to us. At a project level, we have specific practices and procedures to review our estimate of total revenue and cost. Each project team reviews the progress and execution of our performance obligations, which impact the project’s accounting outcome. As part of this process, the project team reviews information such as any outstanding key contract matters, progress towards completion and the related program schedule and identified risks and opportunities. The accuracy of our revenue and profit recognition in a given period depends on the accuracy of our project estimates, which can change from period to period due to a variety of factors including: ● Complexity in original design; ● Extent of changes from original design; ● Different site conditions than assumed in our bid; ● Length of time to complete the project; ● Availability and cost of equipment and materials; ● Subcontractor performance; ● Our ability to recover for additional contract costs. We recognize changes in contract estimates on a cumulative catch-up basis in the period in which the changes are identified. Such changes in contract estimates can result in the recognition of revenue in a current period for performance obligations which were satisfied or partially satisfied in prior periods. Changes in contract estimates may also result in the reversal of previously recognized revenue if the current estimate adversely differs from the previous estimate. Introduction, Transaction Description and Basis of Presentation The following unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information presents the combination of the historical financial information of Conwall Construction Industries Limited and its consolidated subsidiaries (collectively, “Conwall” or the “Company”) and Broad Capital Acquisition Corp. (“BRAC”), after giving effect to the Reorganization, the BRAC Merger and the related transactions contemplated by the Business Combination Agreement (collectively, the “Business Combination”). Following Closing, Holdco will be the parent of CCISB and BRAC and is referred to in this section as the “Combined Company,” subject to the listing conditions and other qualifications described herein. The unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information has been prepared in accordance with Article 11 of Regulation S-X, as amended. It reflects the application of transaction accounting adjustments that are necessary to depict the accounting for the Business Combination. The Combined Company has elected not to present Management’s Adjustments, including projected synergies, cost savings, integration effects or other forward-looking operating adjustments. Description of the Business Combination Pursuant to the Business Combination Agreement, the Business Combination is being effected through a two-step process. First, on July 16, 2026, the share-swap Reorganization made CCISB a wholly owned subsidiary of Holdco. At the Closing, following the completed Reorganization, Conwall DE Sub Inc., a Delaware corporation and wholly owned subsidiary of Holdco (“Merger Sub”), will merge with and into BRAC, with BRAC surviving the merger as a wholly owned subsidiary of Holdco. At the BRAC Merger Effective Time, each issued and outstanding share of BRAC Common Stock that is not redeemed or otherwise cancelled will be converted into the right to receive one newly issued Holdco Ordinary Share. In addition, every ten BRAC Rights issued and outstanding immediately prior to the BRAC Merger Effective Time will be cancelled and converted into one newly issued Holdco Ordinary Share. The fixed existing Conwall equity-holder block is 24,670,924 shares. For the other Closing issuances, 2,910,897 Holdco Ordinary Shares are expected to be received by the BRAC Sponsor and 80,000 by BRAC’s four independent directors, up to 6,969 Holdco Ordinary Shares are expected to be received by BRAC public shareholders that do not redeem, and 1,061,020 Holdco Ordinary Shares are expected to be issued upon conversion of the BRAC Rights. In addition, the actual Loan Conversion Shares and all underwriting settlement and other shares then outstanding are included in Closing capitalization. Completed Company-share issuances are credited without duplication. Under the Business Combination Agreement, as amended, the Company Reorganization Consideration is the fixed net block of 24,670,924 Holdco Ordinary Shares allocated among Ng Boon Teik, Jingji Hu, ENSP Limited, HK Xingfu Capital Holding Limited and Haibiao Deng in Schedule A to the Business Combination Agreement, after giving effect once to the cancellation of 5,329,076 of the original 30,000,000 shares and the identified transfers. Completed issuances, transfers and cancellations are credited in full and will not be repeated. The retained Company Equity Value definition does not recalculate this fixed block. The Payment Spreadsheet reflects its allocation, and the final closing capitalization schedule separately reflects the other Closing issuances. Accounting Treatment of the Business Combination The Business Combination is expected to be accounted for as a capital reorganization, with Conwall treated as the accounting acquirer and BRAC treated as the accounting acquiree. BRAC is a special purpose acquisition company and does not meet the definition of a business for purposes of the expected accounting treatment. Accordingly, the Business Combination is expected to be treated as a reverse recapitalization rather than as a business combination accounted for under the acquisition method. No goodwill or other intangible assets are expected to be recognized as a result of the BRAC Merger. F- 98 Under this accounting treatment, the historical financial statements of Conwall are treated as the historical financial statements of the Combined Company. The net assets and liabilities of BRAC are combined with those of Conwall at historical carrying amounts, subject to the transaction accounting adjustments described below, and the equity structure is recast to reflect the legal capital structure of Holdco following the Closing. Transaction and purpose The unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information gives effect to the proposed business combination in which Conwall DE Sub Inc. merges with and into Broad Capital Acquisition Corp. (BRAC), with BRAC surviving as a subsidiary of Conwall Construction Industries Limited (Holdco). It also reflects the September share cancellation and dividend described in note (g). The information is for illustrative purposes and does not represent the results that would necessarily have occurred had the transactions taken place on the assumed dates or predict future financial position or results. 2. Basis and periods The historical financial information of Conwall and BRAC is prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP. The unaudited pro forma condensed combined balance sheet assumes the transactions occurred on June 30, 2026. The annual and interim statements of operations assume the transactions occurred on April 1, 2025. The presentation assumes a March 31 fiscal year. BRAC annual results comprise the year ended December 31, 2025 plus the quarter ended March 31, 2026 less the quarter ended March 31, 2025. Both interim historical columns cover April through June 2026. Face statements are in U.S. dollars, except share and per-share amounts. Amounts in these notes and supplemental schedules are in U.S. dollars unless otherwise indicated. Minimum redemption assumes no additional redemptions; maximum redemption assumes redemption of all 6,969 remaining public shares. 3. Accounting treatment and estimates The pro forma information assumes that Conwall is the accounting acquirer and that the business combination is a reverse recapitalization of a nonoperating shell. BRAC net assets and liabilities are included at historical carrying amounts, with no goodwill or acquisition-related fair-value step-up. This assumption reflects Conwall’s operating business and approximately 84% of the illustrative share subtotal before underwriting and other additional issuances. The accounting for settlement instruments, transaction costs, intercompany balances, dilution and tax effects is preliminary. Final accounting and closing amounts may differ materially from this presentation. The accounting for underwriting share settlement and the related EPS effects is incomplete, as described in notes (c) and (f); the illustrated capitalization subtotal excludes those shares. (a) Trust liquidation The adjustments eliminate BRAC’s $87,208 trust asset. Under minimum redemption, the balance is transferred to unrestricted cash. Under maximum redemption, it is distributed to holders of all 6,969 remaining public shares. No additional trust earnings are assumed. The separate $291,400 trust over-withdrawal liability is retained and is neither netted against the trust balance nor assumed to be forgiven. (b) Redemption and temporary equity The adjustments eliminate $87,208 of common stock subject to possible redemption. Under minimum redemption, the amount is reclassified to permanent equity. Under maximum redemption, it is eliminated against the trust cash distributed. The illustrative redemption price equals $87,208 divided by 6,969 shares, or approximately $12.51 per share. The scenarios do not establish that all closing or listing conditions will be satisfied. No incremental redemption excise-tax adjustment is included. (c) Underwriter settlement The Deferred Underwriting Fees are $1,500,000 and will be settled at Closing through the issuance of Holdco Ordinary Shares at a price per share equal to the higher of $0.50 and ten times the recent average trading price of BRAC Rights, subject to a 9.9% ownership cap. The underwriter’s net proceeds from sales of those shares may not exceed $1,500,000, and any remaining shares must be returned to Holdco for no consideration. The 3,000,000-share figure is an illustration at the $0.50 floor before application of the variable price and ownership cap, not a fixed issuance. All settlement shares legally outstanding at Closing are included in Closing capitalization even if they may later be returned. The underwriting obligation is separate from the Covered Loan Amount and does not cap loan conversion. The pro forma accounting for the share settlement is incomplete. The preliminary presentation retains a $1,500,000 settlement liability and a $2,055,674 credit to additional paid-in capital from reducing the historical $3,555,674 obligation. Those preliminary entries do not establish that cash settlement is permitted or that the settlement obligation remains payable after the contractual Closing share issuance. Classification, measurement, the related equity or earnings effects and basic and diluted EPS depend on the issued instrument’s terms and the applicable accounting for the proceeds cap and return provisions. The complete Closing capitalization includes all settlement shares legally outstanding, while their EPS treatment is assessed separately. These accounting determinations and the share-price inputs may materially change the preliminary figures presented. (d) Reverse recapitalization and legal capital Pro forma basic shares comprise 24,670,924 Conwall shares, 2,990,897 nonredeemable BRAC shares, 1,061,020 shares issued upon conversion of BRAC rights, 564,078 loan-conversion shares, and either 6,969 or zero remaining public shares. The totals are 29,293,888 shares under minimum redemption and 29,286,919 shares under maximum redemption. Holdco ordinary shares have a par value of $0.0001. BRAC historical common stock and accumulated deficit are eliminated through recapitalization. Conwall retained earnings and accumulated other comprehensive income are preserved, apart from the dividend in note (g). The loan-conversion adjustment reclassifies the carrying amount of the loans to share capital and additional paid-in capital as described in note (j). us_listing_evidence.quote: RELATED PARTY TRANSACTIONS NOTE 5. RELATED PARTY TRANSACTIONS Founder shares On May 7, 2021, the Sponsor purchased 2,875,000 founder shares for an aggregate purchase price of $ 25,000 . The founder shares include an aggregate of up to 375,000 shares subject to forfeiture to the extent that the underwriters’ over-allotment is not exercised in full or in part, so that the number of founder shares will equal, on an as-converted basis, approximately 20 % of the Company’s issued and outstanding shares of ordinary shares after the Initial Public Offering. On May 25, 2021, our sponsor transferred 80,000 insider shares of common stock among our four independent directors, leaving 2,795,000 insider shares held by our sponsor. The initial stockholders have agreed not to transfer, assign or sell any of the common stock (except to certain permitted transferees as disclosed herein) until, with respect to any of the common stock, the earlier of (i) six months after the date of the consummation of a Business Combination, or (ii) the date on which the closing price of the Company’s common stock equals or exceeds $12.00 per share (as adjusted for share subdivisions, share dividends, reorganizations and recapitalizations) for any 20 trading days within any 30-trading day period commencing after a Business Combination, or earlier, if, subsequent to a Business Combination, the Company consummates a subsequent liquidation, merger, share exchange or other similar transaction which results in all of the Company’s stockholders having the right to exchange their common stock for cash, securities or other property. Promissory Note – Related Party On April 16, 2021, the Sponsor issued an unsecured promissory note to the Company, pursuant to which the Company may borrow up to an aggregate principal amount of $ 300,000 , to be used for payment of costs related to the Initial Public Offering. The note is non-interest bearing and payable on the earlier of (i) March 31, 2022 or (ii) the consummation of the Initial Public Offering pursuant to an Amendment to Promissory Note effective September 30, 2021. As of December 31, 2021, the Company had borrowed $ 133,357 under the promissory note with the Sponsor. Following the IPO of the Company on January 13, 2022, a total of $ 133,533 under the promissory note was repaid on January 19, 2022. Related Party Loans In order to finance transaction costs in connection with a Business Combination, the Sponsor or an affiliate of the Sponsor, or certain of the Company’s officers and directors may, but are not obligated to, loan the Company funds as may be required (“Working Capital Loans”). Such Working Capital Loans would be evidenced by promissory notes. The notes may be repaid upon completion of a Business Combination, without interest, or, at the lender’s discretion, up to $ 1,500,000 of the notes may be converted upon completion of a Business Combination into units at a price of $ 10.00 per unit. Such units would be identical to the Private Placement Units. In the event that a Business Combination does not close, the Company may use a portion of proceeds held outside the Trust Account to repay the Working Capital Loans but no proceeds held in the Trust Account would be used to repay the Working Capital Loans. If a REIT owns a corporate subsidiary that is a “qualified REIT subsidiary,” the separate existence of that subsidiary is disregarded for U.S. federal income tax purposes. Generally, a qualified REIT subsidiary is a corporation, other than a TRS, all of the stock of which is owned directly or indirectly by the REIT. Other entities that are wholly-owned by us, including single member limited liability companies that have not elected to be taxed as corporations for U.S. federal income tax purposes, are also generally disregarded as separate entities for U.S. federal income tax purposes, including for purposes of the REIT income and asset tests. All assets, liabilities and items of income, deduction and credit of qualified REIT subsidiaries and disregarded subsidiaries will be treated as assets, liabilities and items of income, deduction and credit of the REIT itself. history.quote: Section 6.7 Indemnification of Employees and Agents of the Corporation; Service at Subsidiaries . The Corporation may, to the extent and in the manner permitted by law, and to the extent authorized from time to time, grant rights to indemnification and to the advancement of expenses to any employee or agent of the Corporation. Any person serving as a director or officer of a subsidiary of the Corporation shall be entitled to the rights to indemnification conferred in this Article VI , and to the advancement of expenses, as defined in Section 6.2, with respect to his or her service at such subsidiary. Any director or officer of a subsidiary is deemed to be serving such subsidiary at the request of the Corporation, and the Corporation is deemed to be requesting such service. This Article VI shall, to the fullest extent permitted by law, supersede any conflicting provisions contained in the corporate governance documents of any other subsidiary of the Corporation. In addition, the Corporation may, to the extent and in the manner permitted by law, and to the extent authorized from time to time, grant rights to indemnification and to the advancement of expenses to individuals with respect to their service as an employee or agent of subsidiaries of the Corporation.

Mr. Wachter’s extensive knowledge of private equity and investment banking provides the Board with the valuable insight of an experienced financial manager.

observations.quote: We may be prohibited under the 1940 Act from conducting certain transactions with our affiliates without the prior approval of the members of our Board (each, a “ Director ”) who are not interested persons and, in some cases, the prior approval of the SEC, including via exemptive order.
